Orchot Tzadikim 26:57: In all these matters and the like of them, teshuvah is very hard. But there is a great remedy to fix everything: let the sinner first reflect on all the matters of teshuvah, and see and understand all its components, and give himself over to do it; and let him do everything for the sake of Heaven with all his strength and all his heart, in private and in public — then the Holy One, blessed be He, will ease the matters of teshuvah for him and guide him on the straight path to teshuvah. For instance, if he fathered a son through forbidden relations, the Holy One, blessed be He, will cut off that offspring and the matter will be forgotten as though it never happened.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:58: And if he robbed money, the Holy One, blessed be He, will provide him with money to repay the one he robbed, and will make him favorable to him and forgive him. And if he did something to a person's body or money, the Blessed Creator will place goodwill and love in that person's heart to forgive him, as it is said (Proverbs 16:7), "when the Lord is pleased with a man's ways, He makes even his enemies be at peace with him." And if the one he robbed is far from him, the Holy One, blessed be He, will bring him near until he pacifies him and he forgives him. And if he does not know the accounting of the money, and does not recognize the people he robbed, the Holy One, blessed be He, will enable him to do something for the public benefit: such as building a bridge, or repairing wells, or building synagogues, or other public needs. And there will be benefit from it for the whole world: for the one he robbed and for others too. And if the one robbed has died, let him return the money to his heirs. If he harmed him bodily or spoke ill of him, let him go to his grave in the presence of ten people and ask forgiveness from the Blessed Lord and from him, and the Holy One, blessed be He, will forgive him.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:59: And our Sages of blessed memory said that teshuvah is withheld from the sinner only because of the wickedness of his own heart. But whoever wishes to draw near to God — He does not close the gates of teshuvah before him, but opens for him the gates of teshuvah and shows him the straight path, as it is written (Psalms 25:8), "good and upright is the Lord, therefore He guides sinners in the way"; and it says (Deuteronomy 4:29), "and you shall seek the Lord your God from there, and you shall find Him, if you seek Him with all your heart and with all your soul"; and it says (ibid. 30:14), "for the thing is very near to you, in your mouth and in your heart, to do it"; and it says (Psalms 145:18), "the Lord is near to all who call upon Him, to all who call upon Him in truth."
Orchot Tzadikim 26:60: Great good has the Holy One, blessed be He, done for people, in that He prepared a path for transgressors and sinners to flee from darkness to light, and does not close the path of teshuvah even if they have greatly transgressed, as it is said (Jeremiah 3:22), "return, backsliding children, I will heal your backslidings." And teshuvah is accepted even if the sinner returns only because of his many troubles, and all the more so if he returns out of fear of Heaven, as it is said (Deuteronomy 4:30), "when you are in distress, and all these things have come upon you... and you return to the Lord your God." And the Holy One, blessed be He, helps those who return to do teshuvah, even in a matter beyond human power, renewing within them a spirit of purity until they attain the matters of teshuvah, as it is said (ibid. 30:2), "and you shall return to the Lord your God and heed His voice." And it says at the end of the matter (ibid. 30:6), "and the Lord your God will circumcise your heart and the heart of your offspring," meaning: even in a matter beyond your own power to attain, the Holy One, blessed be He, will circumcise your heart and give you the strength to do it.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:61: There are four matters in the affairs of teshuvah:
Orchot Tzadikim 26:62: The first: one who returns out of the strength of his own recognition of his God. He is like a servant fleeing his master, who, upon considering the good his master has done him, seeks forgiveness from him of his own accord. And of one like him the verse says (Jeremiah 4:1), "if you will return, Israel, says the Lord, return to Me" — before the punishment comes. And it says (Malachi 3:7), "return to Me, and I will return to you."
Orchot Tzadikim 26:63: The second: one who returns because he has those who rebuke him, shaming him until he returns. He is like a servant who fled his master, and a faithful servant encountered him and rebuked and shamed him for having fled his master, and advised him to return, and assured him that his master would forgive him, and he returned to him and submitted.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:64: The third: when he sees the punishments the Blessed Creator inflicts on whoever strays from His ways, he then returns to the Lord out of fear of His punishment. He is like a servant fleeing his master, who, upon hearing of the punishments given to another who fled from him, then returns.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:65: The fourth: one upon whom punishment and troubles came, and he returned. He is like a fleeing servant whom bandits encountered, who seized him and disciplined him for his flight, and he returned.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:66: And the intelligent man will take hold of his teshuvah in the first manner, and return out of love of His greatness.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:67: Six paths awaken a person's heart to return:
Orchot Tzadikim 26:68: The first: when troubles find a man, let him take it to heart and say: this is only because of my iniquities and my bad ways, and let him return to the Lord, and He will have compassion on him, as it is said (Deuteronomy 31:17), "and many evils and troubles shall come upon them, and he shall say in that day, is it not because our God is not among us that these evils have come upon us?" And this teshuvah is accepted before the Lord — unlike the custom of flesh and blood, where when a man wrongs his fellow, and at a time of his own trouble regrets it and submits to him because he needs his help — this regret is disdainful in his eyes, as Yiftach said (Judges 11:7), "and why have you come to me now, when you are in distress?" But it is among the kindnesses of the Blessed Lord that He accepts teshuvah that comes out of trouble, and is favorably disposed toward it, as it is said (Hosea 14:2), "return, Israel, to the Lord your God, for you have stumbled in your iniquity"; and it is written (Proverbs 3:12), "for whom the Lord loves, He rebukes..."
Orchot Tzadikim 26:69: And if a person does not do teshuvah at the time of his trouble, his punishment is doubled — like a king of flesh and blood: if a man sinned against him and he disciplines him, and the man does not wish to accept his discipline, the king will add to his discipline and make his yoke heavier — so too is the attribute of the Holy One, blessed be He, as it is written (Leviticus 26:18), "and if you will not yet for all this listen to Me, then I will chastise you seven times more." And if he does not consider that the evils come upon him because of his sins, but says "it is mere chance" — there is great wrath upon that man, for he does not believe that his sufferings come because of his iniquities. Know and understand that the Lord's discipline of a person does two good things for him: the first, to atone for his sins, as it is said (Psalms 25:18), "look upon my affliction and my labor, and forgive all my sins." The second, to rebuke him and turn him back from his bad ways, as it is said (Zephaniah 3:7), "surely you will fear Me, you will accept discipline." And if he did not do teshuvah because of his troubles, woe to him, for he bore the suffering and his iniquities were not atoned for. And further, his punishments are doubled, since he does not believe he was disciplined because of his sins.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:70: And whoever trusts in the Blessed Lord must know that troubles are for his own good and to benefit his ultimate end, as it is said (Micah 4:8 — actually 7:8), "do not rejoice over me, my enemy; though I have fallen, I shall rise; though I sit in darkness, the Lord is a light to me." And our Sages of blessed memory said: had I not fallen, I would not have risen; and had I not sat in darkness, there would have been no light for me. Therefore every man, when he has trouble in his body, his money, or his children, should take it to heart to fast at the time of their trouble, as our Sages of blessed memory established (Ta'anit 10a). Therefore, at a time of trouble, let him search his deeds; if he searches and finds no iniquity, it is known that these are sufferings of love (Berachot 5a).
Orchot Tzadikim 26:71: The second: when the days of old age come and he sees the weakening of his strength, let him then think of his end and remember his final days, and return to the Lord, and He will have compassion on him. And whoever does not return in his old age, his punishments will be doubled, as our Sages of blessed memory said (Pesachim 113b): four things the mind cannot bear: a haughty poor man, a lying rich man, an adulterous old man, and a leader who is proud over the community for no reason. And when a person sees his days going, and the structure of his body wasting away and declining, and this is the beginning of the journey he takes toward his eternal home, journeying and traveling day and night — this is a great astonishment: how does he not take to heart to prepare provisions for his great and distant journey? This comes only from a lack of faith,
Orchot Tzadikim 26:72: and they sin greatly against the Blessed Lord in not seeing the light of teshuvah. They are like a sick person who does not feel his illness, and because he does not feel his illness, he does not think about the remedy. So this man does not feel his sins and does not reflect on his end, and therefore does not concern himself with correcting his affairs. And there are people whose entire desire and thoughts and affairs are about their bodily matters, occupying themselves all day with the vanities of the world, and give no portion to Torah and to the fear of the Blessed Lord — how low a level are they in! Therefore whoever walked according to the wantonness of his heart in his youth should, in his old age, take it to heart to drive away from within him the affairs of this world, and devote himself constantly to reflecting on the fear of the Lord, and to seeking Torah and commandments.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:73: The third: when he hears the ethical teaching of the wise and hears those who rebuke him, this awakens his heart to return in teshuvah and accept upon himself all the words of rebuke. And after he accepts, this man merits a great merit, and in a small hour goes out from darkness into great light, and has reward and merit for all the commandments and all the ethical teachings, since he resolved in his mind to accept them upon himself. Happy is he who accepts, for he has merited in a brief hour. And so our Sages of blessed memory said: "and the children of Israel went and did" (Exodus 12:28) — did they do it immediately? Did they not do it only on the fourteenth of the month? Rather, since they accepted upon themselves to do it, the verse credits them as though they had already done it. And our Sages of blessed memory said (Mishnah Avot 3:9): whoever's deeds exceed his wisdom, his wisdom endures, as it is said (Exodus 24:7), "we will do and we will hear."
Orchot Tzadikim 26:74: The explanation of this matter: a person who accepts upon himself with a faithful heart to keep and do all the words of the Torah, and to do as the Sages tell him, and after he has accepted to fulfill everything, seeks out and inquires and asks the Sages what to do — he then has reward even for those commandments and ethical teachings he does not know, since he accepted upon himself and resolved in his heart to do them; just as Israel said at Mount Sinai, "we will do and we will hear," putting doing before hearing (Shabbat 88a). Otherwise it would not be possible for his deeds to exceed his wisdom. And along these lines it is said of Daniel, the precious man, as it is written (Daniel 10:12), "do not fear, Daniel, for from the first day that you set your heart to understand and to afflict yourself before your God, your words were heard." It follows that when a person sets his heart to do good, his words are at once accepted with favor before the Blessed Lord. And whoever does not awaken to return because of those who rebuke him — will not his punishments be doubled?
Orchot Tzadikim 26:75: The fourth: when a person reads the commandments of God, and reads the Prophets and the Writings and the words of the sages of the Talmud, and sees the warnings, the punishments, the commandments, and the pleasant ethical teachings, he should be awakened in his heart and think: "how can I read the matter of the Torah as a mere tale? Rather, I will take the words of the Torah to heart, to keep and do all that I read." As is written of Josiah (2 Kings 22:11), "and it came to pass, when the king heard the words of the book of the Torah, that he tore his garments." And regarding Ezra it is said (Nehemiah 8:9), "for all the people wept when they heard the words of the Torah." And a person who does not set his heart to the words of the Blessed Lord — his transgressions increase because of this, as it is said (Jeremiah 36:24), "and they did not fear, nor tear their garments." And the Sages said (Yerushalmi Berachot 1:2): whoever studies and does not fulfill, it would have been better for him had his afterbirth turned upon his face, and he had never come out into the air of the world. And it is said (Hosea 8:12), "I have written for him the many matters of My Torah, but they were counted as a strange thing"; and it is said (Jeremiah 8:8), "how do you say, we are wise, and the Torah of the Lord is with us? Surely behold, the false pen of the scribes has made it into a lie."
Orchot Tzadikim 26:76: The fifth: when the Ten Days of Repentance arrive, let every person awaken his heart and be shaken before the Day of Judgment. For let him think that all his deeds are written in a book, and at that time God will bring into judgment every deed and everything hidden, whether good or bad. For a person is judged on Rosh Hashanah, and the verdict is sealed on Yom Kippur (Rosh Hashanah 16a). Behold, at the time a person is brought to judgment before a king of flesh and blood, does he not tremble greatly, and take counsel with himself, and think of nothing else but finding merit, how he might be saved from judgment? Therefore how foolish and senseless are those who do not know how their judgment will turn out, yet occupy themselves with idle matters instead of teshuvah, to find favor before the great Judge.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:77: Therefore it is fitting for every God-fearing person to minimize his affairs, and let his thoughts be composed, and set fixed times by day and by night, to be secluded in his rooms and search out and investigate his ways, and to rise early in the watches of the night and occupy himself with the ways of teshuvah. And not do as the world does, fasting and rising early to pray, yet not arraying themselves in battle against their iniquities to remove every disgraceful thing from themselves. For any man who prays and fasts and confesses, yet holds onto his former ways — this is not the path of teshuvah. Rather, a person should be awakened to return in complete teshuvah during the Ten Days of Repentance, which are a time of favor when prayer is heard, as it is said (Isaiah 49:8), "in a time of favor I have answered you, and in a day of salvation I have helped you." And our Sages said (Rosh Hashanah 18a): "seek the Lord while He may be found" (Isaiah 55:6) — these are the ten days between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur. And our Sages of blessed memory said (Yoma 85b) that Yom Kippur atones together with teshuvah; therefore the verse warned us to return and be purified before the Blessed Lord through our teshuvah, and He will atone for us on this day, to purify us.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:78: The sixth: a person should always regard himself as though he is about to die. And he should not say, "when I grow old I will return," lest he die before growing old. Therefore he should at every time direct his intent toward meeting his God, for no person knows his own time. Therefore let him awaken his soul to be pure, to return his spirit in purity to God who gave it to him. And let him examine his deeds at every moment, as Rabbi Eliezer said (Shabbat 153a): return one day before your death. His students said to him: our master, does a person know when he will die? He said to them: let him return today, lest he die tomorrow, and it turns out that all his days are spent in teshuvah, and he will adorn himself every hour as though he were now coming before the great King.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:79: Therefore a person should always worry, even when he is at ease and secure. And let him tremble at the day of death, when he must give a reckoning, and let him confess at every time with a broken and contrite heart as though he were about to die now, and let the fear of Heaven be upon him. And a person should perform a new commandment every day, in case his time of death has arrived; and if he does this, he will not lack a single one of all the commandments. For our Sages of blessed memory said (Kohelet Rabbah 3:24): whoever performs a single commandment close to his death is like one who has fulfilled the whole Torah. Therefore let a person awaken from the sleep of his slumber and rouse himself to understand his end, to adorn himself with the ornaments of the commandments, so as to be before God at every moment.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:80: There are four kinds of teshuvah: teshuvah of the [same] occasion, teshuvah of the fence, teshuvah of the scale, and teshuvah of the [written] verse.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:81: What is teshuvah of the occasion? If he sinned with a woman or by theft, and that same woman or that same iniquity comes his way again, and he was able to sin as before, and he is still in the full strength of his desire and the passion of his inclination, and his heart burns after it and she is favorably disposed toward him, yet he restrains his spirit and severs his desire out of fear of Heaven alone — this is complete teshuvah.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:82: What is teshuvah of the fence? He should not look at the merrymaking of women and maidens, and should not gaze at a married woman's face or at her bosom, nor even at his own wife while she has not yet immersed [after menstrual impurity]. And so he should make a fence for all the commandments. And the Ra'avad, of blessed memory, wrote: we have seen that our Sages were complete pietists, and would fence themselves in with several fences. And there was among them one who separated from his wife after fulfilling the commandment of being fruitful and multiplying. And each one would fence himself according to what he recognized about himself. There is a person who has a desire for one transgression but not for another, such as one who has a desire for lewdness but not for theft, and another who has a desire for theft but not for lewdness. Therefore let each one make fences according to what he sees his own inclination overpowering him in: if his mind is drawn to theft, let him distance himself from accepting deposits and from involvement with others' property; and likewise regarding lewdness, let him fence himself even in what is permitted to him; and so let him make fences for everything. And so our Sages of blessed memory said of Abraham our father, peace upon him, that his inclination made peace with him, and of this it is said (Proverbs 16:7), "when the Lord is pleased with a man's ways, He makes even his enemies be at peace with him." King David waged war with his inclination, and saw that his inclination was not gentle and his nature not easygoing, and he could not overcome it; so he rose up and killed it, as it is said (Psalms 109:22), "and my heart is wounded within me." The meaning: Abraham's inclination was gentle and his nature easygoing and pleasant, and he did not need to wage war with it, as we say (Nedarim 32b): at first Abraham was king only over two hundred and forty-three limbs, and in the end he was made king over two hundred and forty-eight limbs, gaining dominion over his two eyes, his two ears, and the head of his body. But David's inclination was always harsh and strong, and he had to wage war with it every day, and when he saw he could not withstand it, he rose against it and killed it. Some say he killed it through fasting, and some say he separated from his wife entirely, for he saw that through what was permitted it enticed him toward what was forbidden. Whether according to this opinion or that, once he saw his inclination overpowering him, he set his face to subdue it and fight it until he subdued and overcame it.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:83: The fence that is beneficial for subduing the inclination is hunger of the soul — to diminish pleasures and enjoyments in food and drink, only enjoying a good scent; and the enjoyment of hot bathing for one who finds hot water pleasant. And the small amount of food he eats should be well spiced and prepared, so that it be pleasant to him and his soul accept it and be satisfied with a small amount of it. And he should always leave a little less than his need and the full satisfaction of his desire, and drink wine only diluted, so as not to become intoxicated. Of this our Sages of blessed memory said (Gittin 70a): a meal you enjoy — withdraw your hand from it. And there are two benefits in this matter: one, that its eating not harm him, and the second is the subduing of the inclination and the breaking of desire.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:84: And just as we have explained regarding meals, so is the way with all pleasures and enjoyments in the world — that a person not fully satisfy his every craving. And there is no need to say that a person should guard himself from foods he knows are harmful to him, for whoever eats things that harm him, when another food is available to him, is negligent with his own body, since he follows his desire and does not concern himself with the loss of his body. And this is the way and counsel of the evil inclination, which entices him from the way of life to the way of death.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:85: And let every living being know that the evil inclination has only one way, the way of enticement: at first it entices him toward what is permitted, to satisfy his desire, and once he becomes accustomed to satisfying his desire from what is permitted, and his soul is starved to be constantly seething to satisfy its desire, it then entices him toward a light transgression, and from the light to the grave. Therefore be careful, in what is permitted, to make a fence to diminish desire even from what is permitted, and then, if the forbidden should arise in your heart, you can reason from this a fortiori within yourself, and you are assured that you will refrain from the very thought, and how much more so from the deed.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:86: And a person should not afflict his soul so much that his heart weakens and his mind becomes confused, so that his loss exceeds his gain, for he will become idle from Torah — going about idle from weakness, and even at the time he studies he will not be able to be exact as he should and understand the matters, since Torah is acquired only through joy (Shabbat 30b).
Orchot Tzadikim 26:87: And he should not withhold himself from every joy of a commandment and every enjoyment of a commandment, so that his eyes remain open against the evil inclination and he be careful of it, lest he fully satisfy his every desire. And if his heart weakens from eating too little, it is better for him to eat twice a day, a little each time, and not fill his stomach at once. And if he cannot manage to eat twice, let him keep with him some preserve that gladdens the heart, and eat a little of it, and his heart will be strengthened. Also, if he sees for himself that he needs to fast one or two days a week, let him fast according to his own condition, for whoever sits fasting when he needs to is called "holy," provided he does not become idle from Torah and commandments because of it.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:88: Every person can know for himself how to fence himself according to his own affairs. And the head of all fences is that he guard his eyes from what is not his. And if he minimizes his gazing at what is not his, he is called "modest" and "shame-filled," as they said (Shabbat 53b) of that woman who was one-armed, whose husband did not notice it until the day of her death, and they said of him: how modest is this man, that he did not notice his own wife's condition! And if he guards his eyes, it follows that his heart is guarded; and since his heart and eyes are guarded, it follows that his whole self is guarded.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:89: What is teshuvah of the scale? According to the pleasure he derived from the transgression, he should impose suffering on himself through fasting and eating and drinking less; regarding the marital bed and regarding all pleasures, he should reduce them.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:90: What is teshuvah of the [written] verse? If he had relations with a menstruating woman, for which there is excision (karet), or transgressed matters liable for death by the court or flogging, let him accept upon himself to suffer and impose suffering on himself as stated in the Torah. And behold, the Rokeach wrote how one should impose suffering on himself for various transgressions. And so we find in the Talmud that they were accustomed to fasting even for a very light sin, even for a mere utterance. As one sage said (Chagigah 22b): "I am ashamed of your words, House of Shammai" — and for this he sat fasting until his teeth blackened. And so there is a story of Rav Chisda, who said to Rav Huna (Bava Metzia 33a): a student whose teacher needs him — what is the law about standing before him? Rav Huna said to Rav Chisda: "Chisda! Chisda! I do not need you!" — and for this they sat fasting for several days. And so we find with David, that the Divine Presence and the Holy Spirit departed from him for twenty-two years, and every single day he shed tears, and ate his bread with ashes, as it is said (Psalms 102:10), "for I have eaten ashes like bread." He said before Him: Master of the universe! Accept me in complete teshuvah before You, so that You may bring merit to the wicked of the world, as it is said (ibid. 51:15), "I will teach transgressors Your ways" —
Orchot Tzadikim 26:91: let every person learn from David regarding the matter of teshuvah. And so did Adam, the first man: once he saw that death had been decreed because of him, he sat fasting for a hundred and thirty years, and separated from his wife, and placed girdles of fig leaves upon his flesh (Eruvin 18b).
Orchot Tzadikim 26:92: And if a person does teshuvah and returns to his former way, even doing so many times, he can always do teshuvah again. But one should be stricter in a second and third teshuvah than in the first. And we learn in the Yerushalmi (Peah 1:1): whoever was wicked all his days and did teshuvah, the Holy One, blessed be He, accepts him. Rabbi Yochanan said: and not only that, but all his transgressions are turned into merits for him. And in the chapter "Yom HaKippurim" (Yoma 86b): if he did teshuvah out of love, his deliberate sins are turned into merits for him; out of fear, his deliberate sins are turned into unintentional ones. And all those who have no share in the World to Come and are judged in Gehinnom for generation upon generation are specifically those who died in their wickedness; but if they did teshuvah, there is nothing that can stand in the way of repentant sinners. And a person should not think, "since I have sinned, and caused others to sin, I cannot return," and thereby weaken his resolve regarding teshuvah — heaven forbid that he do this! For they said in the chapter "Chelek" (Sanhedrin 102a): even Jeroboam, who sinned and caused others to sin, the Holy One, blessed be He, said to him, "return now," but he did not wish to.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:93: Go and learn from Ahab, king of Israel, who robbed, coveted, and murdered, yet summoned Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, and had himself given lashes three times each day. And he would rise early and stay late in fasting and prayer before the Holy One, blessed be He, and occupied himself with Torah all his days, and did not return to his former deeds, as it is said (1 Kings 21:29), "have you seen how Ahab humbles himself before Me? Because he humbles himself before Me, I will not bring the evil in his days."
Orchot Tzadikim 26:94: And they said in the Pesikta: if he was accustomed to eating at the third hour, he would eat at the sixth hour; if he was accustomed to eating at the sixth hour, he would eat at the ninth hour. And what is "and he went softly" (ibid. verse 27)? Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said: that he went barefoot. Let every person learn from him. And go further and learn from Manasseh son of Hezekiah, who committed the worst abominations in the world, yet the Holy One, blessed be He, accepted him in teshuvah (Pirkei d'Rabbi Eliezer 43). And it was taught before Rabbi Yochanan: Manasseh did teshuvah for thirty-three years, and the Holy One, blessed be He, accepted him (Sanhedrin 103a).
Orchot Tzadikim 26:95: And now, in these generations, when people are very weak in body and do not have the strength they had in earlier times — what should a person do who has sinned all his days through slander and flattery and all the [bad] traits, and was not careful all his days about the actual performance of the commandments, not fulfilling them because he saw no one else fulfilling them from whom to learn, and did not concern himself all his days with praying and reciting the blessings, and likewise with all the commandments — how can he bear suffering in proportion to what he has done? For is there any limit or number to the multitude of transgressions of a person who is not exacting in his deeds?
Orchot Tzadikim 26:96: Therefore a path must be set before people who devote themselves to returning. And there is a difference between one person and another. How so? If this sinner is a man of Torah, and if they burden him too heavily with matters of suffering and fasting, he will be unable to correct his bad traits — one should be lenient with him regarding kinds of fasting and suffering, and instruct him to occupy himself with Torah study intensively. And so they said in Vayikra Rabbah (25:1): if a person stumbled in a transgression and became liable for death at the hand of Heaven, what should he do to live? If he is accustomed to reading one page, let him read two pages; to studying one chapter, let him study two chapters. This teaches that there is atonement through increased study. And let him do kindness and truth, and by this his iniquities will be atoned for, as it is said (Proverbs 16:6), "by kindness and truth iniquity is atoned for." And let him strive to perform every single commandment as stated; and let him strive to bring merit to the many, and do acts of kindness for people, and pray with intent and submission and a torn heart, and seek forgiveness from the Lord for all his transgressions. And let him abstain from laughter and outings and idle talk, and from listening to the world's novelties. And so let him abstain from all such things. And let him gauge for himself, in a precise measure, what he can do and what he can bear alongside his occupation with Torah and commandments. And let him always strive to be submissive to God, and at the very least fast one day a week; and on that day let him free himself from everything in the world, and sit alone by himself, and arrange thoughts in his heart toward God to cleave to Him, and be bitter in spirit for having stood in rebellion against the great King. And let him weep and mourn with a broken heart, and increase supplications, and increase praises. And let him whip himself on that day three times, and at the time he is whipped let him say: "but He, being merciful, forgives iniquity, and destroys not..." through "all His wrath" (Psalms 78:38); and so let him say this at each of the three floggings. And let him do this all his days, until he finds favor before the exalted King.
